c.v: is two threads touching the same memory location with at least one writing and nothing ordering them, which is undefined behaviour. A

is a program whose result depends on the order two threads happen to run in, which may be perfectly defined and still wrong. Atomics remove data races on the object they cover. They remove no race condition by themselves: the check-then-act at the end of this topic is all atomic and all wrong.

You pass with 1, 2 and 3 right and both definitions. Answering 3 with two atomic doubles is a partial pass if you name the torn pair; without that it is a fail, because it is the mistake this topic is about.
An atomic is an object the hardware updates in one indivisible step, so no other thread can see it half written and no two threads can lose an update to each other.
on it is one indivisible operation, not the read, add and write a plain

The problem it solves is the cost and the reach of a mutex. A mutex protects any invariant of any size, and it costs a system call when contended and blocks whoever loses. An atomic covers one object of one word, needs no waiting at all, and on x86-64 an increment is one instruction,
. So a counter, a shutdown flag or a pointer swap wants an atomic; anything that keeps two values in step wants a mutex, because two atomics read one after the other give a pair that never existed.
The mechanism has two halves, and interviews ask about the second. Atomicity is indivisibility. The

I measured what each order compiles to, and a relaxed store, a release store and every load are one

What it costs is that atomics are hard to combine. Two atomic steps are not one atomic step, so

Read the table twice. Every load is the same instruction whatever you ask for, and so is every read-modify-write: on this processor the ordering you get for free is already almost sequential consistency. The single difference is the sequentially consistent store, which becomes a locked exchange instead of a plain move. So on x86-64 the memory order argument is nearly free, and writing

everywhere buys you one instruction on stores while costing you the guarantee that makes your reasoning simple. On ARM, where the hardware reorders more, the same table has a fence in most rows and the choice is worth making. This is why
says to distrust your hardware and compiler combination: code that is correct by accident on x86 breaks on the robot's ARM board.

When is an atomic enough? When the shared thing is one object and every operation on it is one of the atomic operations. A message counter, a sequence number, a shutdown flag, a pointer swapped for another. When is it not? When the invariant spans more than one object, which is the odometry accumulator from the threads topic: three fields that have to move together. Two atomics cannot do that, because between your two loads another thread can change both.
puts it plainly: don't reach for lock-free programming unless you have to, and the reason is that the reasoning gets hard long before the performance gets good.

One more cost, which surprises people who think an atomic is free. An atomic lives in a cache line of 64 bytes, and a line belongs to one core at a time when it is being written. Four counters declared next to each other share one line, so four threads incrementing their own counter still fight over one line, a phenomenon called
. The same four, each padded to its own line with

If you need a real snapshot there are three honest answers. Put the three numbers in a struct under one mutex, and accept the lock. Put them in one atomic struct if they fit in the lock-free size, which two
counters would and three 64-bit ones would not. Or keep a version number that a reader checks before and after reading the fields, which is the

Every access in this program is atomic. It has no data race, ThreadSanitizer says nothing about it, and it is still wrong:

blocks.text: 8 of 8 threads believed they were the first

c.v: The 5 millisecond sleep stands for the work a real claimant does between deciding it is first and recording that it was: opening the log file, loading the map, connecting to the driver. It also makes the output the same on every run, and the margin is measured rather than assumed: a program that records when each of the eight threads gets past the latch reports 86 to 197 microseconds between the first and the last over eight runs, so the 5 millisecond window is 25 to 60 times the spread. A busier machine that stretched that spread to half a millisecond would still leave the window ten times over. Shorten the window and the bug gets rarer, not smaller: with no sleep at all this same program printed 1 of 8 on every one of ten runs, which is what a bug looks like the week before it reaches a customer.
The defect is not in either operation. It is that there are two of them. Between the
any number of threads can run the same
, and an atomic promises nothing about what happens between two of its operations. This is a

without a data race, which is why the tool that found the threads topic's bugs is silent: ThreadSanitizer looks for unordered accesses to the same location, and here every access is ordered and atomic.
The fix is to make the test and the claim one operation:
writes the new value and returns the old one, in one indivisible step, so exactly one thread can see

c.v: The rule to carry out of this topic: an atomic makes one operation indivisible, and a sequence of atomic operations is not one operation. Before you write two of them in a row, ask what another thread may do in between, and if the answer matters, reach for one operation that does both, or for a mutex.
